text: On December first, 1984, NASA and the FAA intentionally crashed a remotely piloted Boeing 720 at Edwards Air Force Base.
The aircraft was an obsolete four-engine Boeing 720 obtained from the FAA.
The purpose was to test a fuel additive called FM-9 anti-misting kerosene to reduce post-crash fire, and to gather structural data and seat and restraint test data.
No flight crew was aboard on the final flight; the airplane was flown from a ground cockpit.
Before the final flight, the team flew fourteen test flights with crews aboard.
They practiced sixty-nine approaches to the impact site.
They accumulated sixteen hours and twenty-two minutes of remote control.
There were ten remote takeoffs and thirteen remote landings.
In practice, the airplane was never flown lower than a hundred and fifty feet above ground toward the impact site.
Below a hundred and fifty feet, the airplane was committed to impact.
At the decision point, the airplane arrived slightly right of centerline.
The pilot judged altitude sufficient and continued.
The left wing hit first, short of the wing cutters.
The left wing dropped and contacted the ground first, short of the wing cutters.
The nose swung left and skidded at about a forty-five degree angle.
The damaged right wing broke off and folded over.
A cutter struck the right inboard engine.
A massive fuel leak ignited.
The right wing broke off and folded over.
The right wing broke off and folded over.
The fuselage was engulfed in a massive fuel-fed fireball.
The fire took more than an hour to fully extinguish.
Exterior and internal film documentation indicates the resulting fire diminished within nine seconds.
The fuselage sustained relatively little damage during the duration of the fire.
Fire that later damaged the aircraft interior resulted from burning fuel entering the fuselage during the slideout.
Fuel appeared to have entered through a forward cargo door and/or openings made by passage of wing cutters through the fuselage structure.
Burning fuel inside the fuselage ruptured by wing cutters was responsible for the long-term fire which entered the cabin by burning through the floor.
Cabin cameras showed crash test dummies shaken and small panels falling, but the seats remained attached to the floor.
The Controlled Impact Demonstration marked the end of FAA attempts to order airlines to use the anti-misting additive.
FAA requirements for the additive were cancelled.
Full-scale demonstration in a real-world flight environment showed the modified anti-misting fuel was ineffective in reducing the propagation or intensity of fire.
Small-scale ground tests had indicated the anti-misting additive would be effective in reducing post-crash fires.
Proponents argued the modified fuel prevented a hotter, more catastrophic fire during the test.
The antimisting additive tested was not sufficient to prevent a post-crash fire in all circumstances.
About one-quarter of the passengers would have survived, and several changes to equipment in the passenger compartment were needed.
